sheet.howExamined: Usually one of the last three questions on the M3 paper. The common shape is a four-mark drawing from five statistics, two of which must be calculated first, followed by a one-mark reasoning part; the alternative is a pair of box plots with a two-mark 'make two comparisons' instruction. Marks are split: one for each calculated value, one for the format of the plot and one for plotting all five values. The reasoning mark is consistently the hardest mark on the paper.

noteBlocks.text: Box plots: five numbers, one picture

noteBlocks.md: A box plot is the five-figure summary drawn on a scale: **minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum**. The box holds the middle half of the data, the line inside it is the median, and the two whiskers reach the extremes. It is the fastest way to compare two sets of data, which is why CCEA almost always follows a box plot with the instruction to make two comparisons.

The left-hand edge of the box
The middle of the whole scale

noteBlocks.title: Not on the formula sheet
noteBlocks.md:
$\text{maximum} = \text{minimum} + \text{range}$ and $\text{minimum} = \text{maximum} - \text{range}$

$\text{UQ} = \text{LQ} + \text{IQR}$ and $\text{LQ} = \text{UQ} - \text{IQR}$

Each of the four sections of the plot holds a quarter of the data. None of this is printed anywhere in the exam.

noteBlocks.prompt: From the picture above, what is the interquartile range of the waiting times, in minutes?
noteBlocks.explain: The width of the box: $45 - 26 = 19$ minutes. The range, whisker to whisker, is 56.

noteBlocks.title: Why the long whisker holds no more data
noteBlocks.md: Each of the four sections is a quarter of the values, so a wide section means the values there are spread out, not that there are more of them. The long right-hand whisker above covers the slowest quarter of the patients, thinly scattered between 45 and 68 minutes.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box plot's right-hand whisker is three times as long as its box. What does that tell you?
options: The slowest quarter is spread out
There are more values in the whisker
The median is too high
noteBlocks.answer: The slowest quarter is spread out
noteBlocks.explain: Every section holds a quarter of the data, so a longer section means those values are more spread out, not that there are more of them.

noteBlocks.md:
A CCEA question rarely hands you five positions. It hands you a mixture, like this:

maximum 96%, median 40%, lower quartile 28%, range 84%, interquartile range 24%.

Three of those are **positions** on the scale. Two are **widths**: a range of 84 does not mean anyone scored 84%.

So before drawing: minimum $= 96 - 84 = 12$, and upper quartile $= 28 + 24 = 52$. Each of those carries its own mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: A data set has maximum 96 and range 84. What is the minimum?
noteBlocks.explain: $96 - 84 = 12$. The range is the whole distance from the smallest value to the largest.

noteBlocks.prompt: The lower quartile is 28 and the interquartile range is 24. What is the upper quartile?
noteBlocks.explain: $28 + 24 = 52$. The interquartile range is the width of the box, so it is added on to the left-hand edge.

noteBlocks.title: Drawing and Reading Box Plots
noteBlocks.why: The drawing routine end to end. Watch the order: the box between the quartiles first, then the median line, then the whiskers.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the video, what is drawn first?
noteBlocks.answer: The box between the two quartiles
noteBlocks.explain: Yes. The box fixes the scale of the drawing, and the median line and whiskers are added to it.
options: The box between the two quartiles
The whiskers
The median line on its own

noteBlocks.md:
Two box plots on the same scale is an invitation to make **two comparisons**, and the two marks are deliberately different: one for an **average**, one for **spread**.

- Average: compare the **medians**, then say what it means. *Moira's median is greater, so callers there waited longer on average.*
- Spread: compare the **interquartile ranges**, then say what it means. *Larne's interquartile range is smaller, so its waits were more consistent.*

Two sentences about medians earn one mark, not two. A sentence that only quotes numbers earns none.

noteBlocks.prompt: Fill the gap: two box plots are compared with one sentence about an average and one about ______.
noteBlocks.explain: Spread. The words spread, variation or consistent are what the second comparison mark is looking for.

options: One
Two
None
noteBlocks.explain: One mark is for an average and the other for spread, so a second median sentence adds nothing. Compare the interquartile ranges for the second mark.

noteBlocks.text: Why the interquartile range, and what a sample can tell you

noteBlocks.md:
When a question asks **why** the interquartile range represents a data set better than the range, it is asking about **that** data set. The competition scores above are a good example: one entry of 96% sits far above the rest and drags the range up to 84. The interquartile range of 24 ignores it.

The sentence that earns the mark names the value. "The interquartile range is not affected by extremes" is true, and it earns nothing.

A box plot of a **sample** describes the sample. Another sample would give different quartiles, so a comparison of two samples is evidence about those samples, not proof about the whole population.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which reason would earn the mark for a data set whose maximum is 96% when everything else is below 60%?
options: The 96% is far above the rest, so it stretches the range but leaves the interquartile range alone
The interquartile range is not affected by extreme values
The interquartile range is a more accurate measure
noteBlocks.answer: The 96% is far above the rest, so it stretches the range but leaves the interquartile range alone
noteBlocks.explain: It names the value in this data set. The other two are general statements, and neither scored in November 2025.

noteBlocks.md:
Read all five values, the range and the interquartile range off a box plot.
Turn a range or an interquartile range into the value it hides.
Compare two plots with one sentence on average and one on spread.

The usual shape is a four-mark plot drawn from five statistics, two of which you work out first, then a one-mark explain-why; sometimes it is two printed plots and make two comparisons. The first marks are the calculated values, so list all five before drawing. The last is the plot itself, ruled and complete. Stuck: name the value unlike the rest and say what it does to the range.

workedExamples.stem:
A vet recorded the masses of the dogs brought into a clinic in one week.

The minimum mass was 4 kg. The median was 15 kg. The upper quartile was 26 kg. The range was 38 kg. The interquartile range was 15 kg.

Draw a box plot for these masses on the scale below. [4]

figure.alt: A blank scale for a box plot, marked in kilograms from 0 to 50 in steps of 10 with small squares of 2 kg.

steps.working: Sort the five numbers into positions and widths: the minimum, the median and the upper quartile are positions on the scale; the range and the interquartile range are widths.
steps.decision: Only three of the five can be plotted as they stand. Deciding which is which before drawing anything is what separates full marks from zero here.

options: Because a range is a distance between two values, not a place on the scale
Because the range is always the largest of the five numbers
Because widths are plotted at the right-hand end of the box plot
whyMenu.explain: A range of 38 kg does not mean a dog weighed 38 kg. It means the heaviest and lightest differ by 38 kg, so it has to be combined with a value that is a position.

steps.decision: The range reaches from the minimum, so add it on. This is the first of the two calculated values, and it carries its own mark.
The interquartile range is the width of the box, and the upper quartile is its right-hand edge, so the left-hand edge is that width back down the scale.

steps.working: Five values: minimum 4, lower quartile 11, median 15, upper quartile 26, maximum 42. Draw the box from $11$ to $26$, the median line at $15$, and one whisker out to each end.
steps.decision: Ruler, dark lines, one line inside the box. Faint pencil and extra lines inside the box both cost marks in the November 2025 report.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Box plot with minimum 4, lower quartile 11, median 15, upper quartile 26, maximum 42, all in kilograms.

workedExamples.stem:
The box plot shows the waiting times at a walk-in centre one morning.

Work out the interquartile range, and state what fraction of the patients waited longer than the upper quartile. [3]

figure.alt: A box plot on a scale of minutes from 0 to 80, labelled Waiting times at the walk-in centre: the left whisker starts at 12, the box runs from 26 to 45 with a vertical line inside it at 34, and the right whisker ends at 68.

steps.working: The box runs from $26$ to $45$, so LQ $= 26$ and UQ $= 45$.
steps.decision: The edges of the box are the quartiles; the ends of the whiskers are the minimum and the maximum. Naming each of the five parts before reading anything stops the two being mixed up.
The interquartile range is the width of the box. The range, whisker to whisker, would be a different answer entirely.

steps.working: Three quarters of the patients waited less than the upper quartile, so a quarter waited longer.
steps.decision: The three quartiles cut the data into four groups of equal size. Everything to the right of the box is one of those four groups.

options: Because the quartiles cut the data into four equal groups, and the right-hand whisker holds one of them
Because the right-hand whisker is the longest part of the plot
Because the upper quartile is three quarters of the way along the scale
whyMenu.explain: The four sections of a box plot hold equal numbers of values even though they look nothing like the same width.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Interquartile range 19 minutes; a quarter, or 25%, of the patients waited longer than the upper quartile.

workedExamples.stem:
The box plots show how long calls waited to be answered at two contact centres, Larne and Moira, on the same day.

Make two comparisons between the two centres. [2]

figure.alt: Two box plots on the same scale of minutes from 0 to 24. Larne: whiskers at 1 and 15, box from 4 to 8, with the line inside the box at 6. Moira: whiskers at 2 and 20, box from 5 to 16, with the line inside the box at 11.

steps.working: Medians: Larne $6$, Moira $11$. Interquartile ranges: Larne $8 - 4 = 4$, Moira $16 - 5 = 11$.
steps.decision: Write the four numbers down first. One comparison will be about an average and the other about spread, so one pair of each is needed.

steps.working: Moira's median is greater, so callers at Moira waited longer on average.
steps.decision: The mark is not for noticing that 11 is bigger than 6. It is for saying what that means for a caller, in the words of the question.

steps.working: Larne's interquartile range is smaller ($4$ against $11$ minutes), so the waits at Larne were more consistent.
steps.decision: The second mark needs a spread word: spread, variation or consistent. Summer 2024 reports that most candidates managed the median sentence and few managed this one.

options: Because an interquartile range is a measure of spread, so the sentence must say how much the times varied
Because the second comparison must always mention the maximum
Because a smaller interquartile range means a smaller median
whyMenu.explain: The two marks are deliberately one average and one spread. A second sentence about medians earns nothing.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Moira has the greater median, so callers there waited longer on average; Larne has the smaller interquartile range, so its waiting times were more consistent.

options.text: The midpoint of the range
options.feedback: The median is the middle value, not the middle of the scale; the two agree only by coincidence.

options.text: The interquartile range

findTheMistake.stem: A data set has minimum 5, median 24, upper quartile 33, range 52 and interquartile range 16. Séan was asked to draw the box plot. Here is his plan.
studentWorking: So minimum 5, lower quartile 16, median 24, upper quartile 33, maximum 52.
Draw the box between the two quartiles, the median line inside, whiskers to each end.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 treats all five printed numbers as positions on the scale. Two of them are widths: the range is how far the maximum is from the minimum, and the interquartile range is how wide the box is. Sorting them in line 2 hides the problem rather than fixing it, so line 3 puts the interquartile range where the lower quartile belongs and the range where the maximum belongs.
correction: Five values: minimum 5, lower quartile 17, median 24, upper quartile 33, maximum 57.
Then draw the box, the median line and the two whiskers with a ruler.
findTheMistake.feedback: As written this scores 1 of 4: the shape of the plot is right, so the format mark stands, but neither calculated value is there and the plotting mark goes. The November 2025 report says over half the candidature plotted the five given values with no idea what they represented. Work out the maximum (57) and the lower quartile (17) first.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife is comparing the two contact centres from their box plots (Larne: median 6, IQR 4; Moira: median 11, IQR 11). She writes two comparisons.
studentWorking: 1st comparison: Larne's median is 6 and Moira's median is 11.
2nd comparison: Larne's interquartile range is 4 and Moira's interquartile range is 11.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Both lines quote values without comparing anything. A comparison mark needs a statement: which is greater, and what that means for a caller. Line 2 has the same fault, and it also never uses a word for spread.
correction: 1st comparison: Moira's median is greater ($11$ against $6$ minutes), so callers at Moira waited longer on average.
2nd comparison: Larne's interquartile range is smaller ($4$ against $11$ minutes), so the waits at Larne were more consistent.
findTheMistake.feedback: As written this scores 0 of 2. The readings are correct, which is the hard part; adding the two clauses 'so callers waited longer on average' and 'so the waits were more consistent' turns them into the comparisons the scheme rewards. Summer 2024 M3 Q26 reports the same gap: values quoted without meaning.

findTheMistake.stem: A box plot of competition scores has minimum 12, lower quartile 28, median 40, upper quartile 52, maximum 96, all percentages. Rhys is asked why the interquartile range represents this data better than the range.
studentWorking: The interquartile range is not affected by extreme values.
The range is affected by extreme values.
So the interquartile range is better.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Every line is true in general and none of them mentions this data set. The mark is for pointing at the feature that makes the difference here: one score of 96% far above the rest, which on its own fixes the range at 84.
correction: The middle half of the scores lies between $28\%$ and $52\%$.
One score of $96\%$ sits far above the rest and stretches the range to $84$.
The interquartile range of $24$ describes the middle half and is untouched by that one score.
findTheMistake.feedback: As written this scores 0 of 1. In November 2025 this was the poorest response on the entire M3 paper, and the same mark on M4 was earned by 9% of candidates, because generic contrasts like these were not accepted. One sentence naming the 96% would have earned it.

findings.wentWrong: The strongest worked out the minimum (3) and the upper quartile (20) from the clues and drew accurately; many got the minimum only; weaker candidates plotted the five numbers as printed. The reasoning mark came from the median being 14.
findings.rule: Some of the five values must be calculated from the clues before drawing.

findings.asked: Draw a box plot and interpret it.
findings.wentWrong: Most found the minimum but struggled with the upper quartile of 20; some drew without a ruler. Interpretation via the median was fine.

findings.asked: Box plot needing two values calculated first; then explain why the IQR suits this data.
findings.wentWrong: Over half plotted the five printed numbers with no calculation. The explanation was the worst-answered item on the paper: generic contrasts of range and IQR did not score; the mark needed the observation that the range was inflated by the one very high value (98%).
findings.rule: A reason must point at the feature of this data set.

findings.asked: Box plot with two values to calculate; explain why the IQR is more suitable.
findings.wentWrong: Common part-scores: minimum right but 30 taken as the LQ, or LQ right with minimum taken as 0. Extra lines inside the box and very faint pencil were noted. Only 9% earned the explanation mark - generic answers about extremes were not enough.
findings.rule: Draw dark, clean lines; cite the extreme value in the data.

insight.ruleToRemember: Work out any missing statistics from the clues before drawing; draw dark, clean lines; compare with one average and one spread statement in context; a 'why' answer must name the feature of the given data.
